schools.summary: Gill sets the thesis: against Zophar's claim that the prosperity of the wicked is only for a short time, Job proves the contrary, that in many instances it continues as long as they live, that they die in it, and their posterity enjoy it after them.

Henry hears a man commending his case and discourse to his friends' compassion, asking leave to speak and to be marked, and insisting his complaint is not to man but to God, before whom they stand upon even terms.

Clarke maps the whole chapter: Job puzzled by the unequal distribution of temporal goods, showing the wicked live long and prosper in families, flocks, and substance while defying God, yet are reserved for a day of wrath.

Ellicott fixes the turn in the argument: having declared his belief in a retribution to come (ch. 19), Job now traverses Zophar's contention directly, to show that even in this life there is not the retribution the friends maintained.

themes: the frame of the whole speech

schools.summary: Gill takes 'hear diligently my speech' as a plea for closest attention to the oration on the prosperity of the wicked, that his friends might weigh the force of his reasoning and own that truth lay on his side.

Keil and Delitzsch: the friends do not recognise the mystery but wound him with frivolous accusations; let their attention supply the place of their consolations, and let them bear with him uninterrupted. Ellicott: 'Listen to my words, and let that be the consolation you give me.'

Wesley: if you have no other comfort, at least afford me this; Clarke reads 'consolations' as 'retractations' (the root also meaning to repent, whence the Vulgate 'and repent'), or takes the verse ironically.

outliers.note: Renders 'let this be your consolations' as 'let this be your retractations,' the Hebrew root signifying not only to comfort but to change one's mind and repent (so the Vulgate 'agite paenitentiam,' Coverdale 'amend yourselves').

schools.summary: Gill reads 'suffer me that I may speak' as an entreaty for patience to hear him out to the end; several Jewish commentators render it 'bear me,' though what he says sit heavy upon them.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'Suffer me, and I will speak, and after I have spoken thou mayest mock,' marking the turn to the singular, the leave to scoff aimed at the last speaker who provoked him.
Wesley keeps the clauses bald: 'Speak, without interruption. Mock, if I do not defend my cause with solid arguments, go on in your scoffs.'

themes: suffer me that I may speak
the singular address to the mocker

schools.summary: Gill: Job's complaint is not to his friends nor any man but to God, of whom he thinks himself hardly dealt with, and to whom he had appealed to know the reason of the contention.
Clarke renders the cry 'Alas for me! is it not with a man that I speak? why should not my spirit be troubled?'; Wesley: 'my complaint is to God only; and if it were to man, have I not cause?'
Ellicott paraphrases fully: not to man but to God he complains, venturing to ask why His justice is so tardy, a problem which when he remembers it troubles him so that horror takes hold on his flesh.
Gill glosses 'mark me' as 'look at me,' not at his person but at his sorrows, whether any sorrow was like his, and at the words he was about to say of God's providence toward good and bad men.

Clarke: compare my former and present state and be astonished, put your hand upon your mouth and keep silent, the recognised token of silence, as the Egyptian god Harpocrates is shown with finger on lip; Wesley: consider, and be silent.

Gill lists what the remembering may be: the iniquities of his youth, his former prosperity reviewed against his misery, the evil tidings of his losses, or the instances of providence he is about to relate.

Henry ties the trembling to the terrible day of his stripping and boils and the hard speeches of his friends; the providences of God are sometimes astonishing even to wise and good men, bringing them to their wits' end.
Clarke: 'I tremble at the thought of entering into a detail on such a subject; my very flesh trembles'; Wesley: 'the very remembrance of what is past fills me with dread and horror.'

themes: when I remember I am afraid
trembling takes hold of my flesh

schools.summary: Gill hears the question put either to God, that a holy Being suffers such wretches to live while a God-fearing man is afflicted, or to the friends, challenging them to reconcile the fact with their principle; why do the wicked live at all, or live 'lively' and thriving?

Henry takes the three verbs as the height, breadth, and length of prosperity: they live, become old, are mighty in power; and asks the reasons, not that God forsakes the earth but that the measure of iniquity is not full, this being the day of patience and the proof that retribution belongs to another world.

Clarke drives it at the friends' maxim: many wicked live long and prosperously and die in peace, a daily fact none can deny; how then reconcile it with their doctrine that the wicked are invariably punished in this life?
Gill: not seed sown but the wicked man's children, numerous and happily settled, seen with his own eyes while yet living, prospering near him or in like circumstances.

Ellicott: they leave their power to their children after them (Ps. 17:14), which contradicts what Eliphaz (15:34), Bildad (18:19), and Zophar (20:10) had all said; Keil and Delitzsch set the clause at the head of the strophe of the undisturbed household.
Clarke: they see their children and children's children settled in the land, so that their generations, even the posterity of the wicked, are not cut off.
Henry: prosperity complete and consummate, the family multiplied and built up, put first as giving both a pleasant enjoyment and a pleasing prospect.

themes: their seed established in their sight
the posterity of the wicked continue

schools.summary: Gill: safe from fear of enemies and robbers, or 'their houses are peace,' free from fear both within doors and without.
Clarke: 'neither is the rod of God upon them' means simply that they are not afflicted as other men, the very stroke Job feels being the one they escape.
Ellicott hears an open collision with the friends: on the contrary Zophar had said 'a fire not blown should consume him' (20:26) and Bildad that 'destruction should dwell in his tabernacle' (18:15).
Henry: whereas Zophar spoke of continual frights and terrors, Job says their houses are safe from danger and from the fear of it, so far from God's wounds that they feel not even the rod.

themes: their houses are safe from fear
the rod of God not upon them

schools.summary: Gill: the increase of cattle, the riches of that age lying in living stock, one part put for the whole; a man was reckoned happy when these brought forth abundantly.

Keil and Delitzsch defend the natural reading: 'his bull' is the male and the verb means to gender or impregnate, against Rosenmuller after Bochart, who on the Septuagint and Jerome took it of the female that conceives; the Targum renders it 'impregnating.'
Clarke keeps the plain sense: the bull passes over the cow and fails not, their flocks multiply, bring forth in time, and none is barren.
Henry: they are rich and thrive, not a cow casting her calf, the very fruitfulness promised to obedience (Exod. 23:26; Deut. 7:14).

debates.question: Is the beast of the first clause the male bull that impregnates, or the female that conceives?

sides.position: the male bull, 'gendereth' meaning to impregnate
the female that conceives, following the Septuagint and Jerome
holders: Rosenmuller and Bochart (as reported by Keil and Delitzsch)

themes: their bull gendereth and faileth not
the philology of the male beast

schools.summary: Gill: the 'little ones' are the man's own family, likened to a flock for their numbers, sent into the streets to play and dance, under no restraint and no care for a sober upbringing.
Clarke leaves the reference open, whether the young of the flocks or the children; either way, healthy and vigorous, they dance for joy.
Henry: a merry, jovial life, the little ones sent to sport themselves; yet an instance of vanity too, with none of the care Abraham took to teach his household the way of the Lord (Gen. 18:19).

themes: they send forth their little ones like a flock

schools.summary: Gill assigns the instruments to the parents who play while the children dance, or (with Jarchi and Aben Ezra) reads that they lift up the voice with tabret and harp, joining vocal and instrumental music.

Clarke details the instruments (timbrel a drum like the tom-tom, the 'organ' a syrinx or pipe), commends Mr. Good's 'they trip merrily to the sound of the pipe,' and notes this is spoken of the children of those who say to God, 'Depart from us.'
Henry: the parents pipe and the children dance after their pipe; sensual pleasures are all the delights of carnal people, and as the men are, so they breed their children.

themes: they take the timbrel and harp
rejoice at the sound of the organ
mirth handed to the next generation

schools.summary: Gill reads 'in wealth' as 'in good,' earthly good and not spiritual; and flags the textual point, that the received reading follows the Keri 'they spend their days,' while the written text (Cetib) is 'they become old.'

Keil and Delitzsch render 'they enjoy their days in prosperity, and in a moment go down to Sehol'; Ellicott catches the sting of 'in a moment,' that they go down to death without the lingering tortures Job had to undergo.

Clarke weighs the variant and prefers 'they grow old / wear out,' since Job's argument gains strength if the wicked are not cut off suddenly; Wesley: 'they do not die of a lingering and tormenting disease.'

debates.question: Does the disputed verb say the wicked 'spend their days in wealth' or 'grow old / wear out' in prosperity?

sides.position: 'spend their days in wealth' (the received reading of the AV and Vulgate)
'grow old / wear out' in prosperity, the reading that most strengthens Job's argument

themes: they spend their days in wealth
in a moment go down to the grave
a painless death spared Job's tortures

schools.summary: Gill traces the insolence to the wealth, which makes men proud and forsake their Creator; the words, if not openly uttered, are conceived in the mind and proclaimed by their lives.

Ellicott corrects the connective: not 'therefore they say' but 'Yet they said unto God, Depart from us,' the atheism defying the very mercies that provoke it; Keil and Delitzsch render the same adversative, 'and yet they said to God, Depart from us.'

Clarke gives the speech as the language of their conduct ('thy ways are painful, thy ways are spiritual, we wish to live after the flesh'); Wesley: sometimes in words, but commonly in their thoughts and the language of their lives.

themes: we desire not the knowledge of thy ways

schools.summary: Gill: what is there in God that should oblige us to serve him? the question full of atheism, treating God as a mere idol, doing neither good nor evil, having forsaken the earth.
Clarke gives the worldly voice: what allegiance do we owe? what profit from prayer? our kingdom is of this world; and those who never pray know nothing of its benefits.
Henry: they speak slightingly of God (a mere cipher), hardly of religion (a drudgery), highly of themselves, breaking both bonds of duty and interest; 'it is vain to serve God' (Mal. 3:14).

themes: what is the Almighty that we should serve him
the two bonds of duty and interest

schools.summary: Gill: their good is in their possession but not in their power to keep or carry away; God who gave it can take it, so it might have profited them to serve him.

Keil and Delitzsch: not by their own hand, but a gift from the very God they deny, which is the mystery Job cannot bring to view; 'the counsel of the wicked be far from me' is his disavowal. Ellicott agrees it constitutes the mystery, or reads it as a supposed objection with the last clause Job's repudiation.

Clarke: God only lends them his bounty, and 'far be it from me to advocate the cause of the wicked'; Wesley: their wealth is not obtained nor kept by their own might but by God's favour, so Job is far from approving their course.

themes: their good is not in their hand
prosperity a gift from the God they deny
the counsel of the wicked far from me

schools.summary: Gill: Job returns to the settled prosperity of the wicked, taking up Bildad's word and asking how often the candle (their outward happiness) is really put out, whether the instances be frequent or few.

Henry hears a challenge: how often do you see it, and not as often burnt to the socket? perhaps as many notorious sinners end in pomp as in misery, so no verdict can be drawn from a man's outward condition.
Wesley: 'I grant this happens often, though not constantly, as you affirm'; Clarke: oftentimes the wicked's rejoicing is short and God portions out misery in his anger.
Ellicott offers both, a concession or a rhetorical 'how often do we see this?'; Keil and Delitzsch take the second firmly, 'How rarely is the light of the wicked put out.'

debates.question: Is 'how oft is the candle of the wicked put out?' a concession that it happens, or a rhetorical question meaning 'how seldom!'?

sides.position: a concession that the wicked are sometimes cut off, but not always
a rhetorical question meaning 'how rarely / how seldom,' all but denying it

themes: how oft is the candle of the wicked put out

schools.summary: Gill keeps the interrogative running: how often are they as stubble before the wind, how often does God make them as chaff before the storm?

Clarke hears the winnowing of judgment, the fan that purges the floor and burns the chaff (cf. Ps. 1:4), the Hebrew picturing men carried off by a furious storm and borne away as booty by desert robbers.
Keil and Delitzsch render the straw and chaff, and set it against the friends' law that virtue is necessarily rewarded and sin punished, which is the position Job contends against.

themes: against the law of strict retribution

schools.summary: Gill takes it as an objection Job foresees and grants: be it so the wicked prosper in their persons, God reserves the punishment of their iniquity for their children when the measure is full.
Henry: God lays up the father's iniquity for the children to make them beggars, sealing their sins among his treasures (Deut. 32:34) and punishing them while the cursed riches remain in their hands.

Clarke grounds it in Exod. 20:5, the children who copy the parents or inherit ill-gotten goods; Wesley reads 'layeth up' as a treasuring of wrath against the day of wrath (Rom. 2:5), punishing him in person and posterity.
Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch read the first line as the friends' maxim placed in Job's mouth, and the second as his retort, 'Let him repay it to the man himself, that he may know it and feel it.'

debates.question: Is 'God layeth up his iniquity for his children' Job's own view, or the friends' claim which he quotes to rebut?

sides.position: Job's own concession that God punishes the children and posterity
the friends' maxim which Job quotes only to reject, demanding the sinner himself be repaid

themes: God layeth up his iniquity for his children
let him repay it to himself

schools.summary: Gill reads the verbs as Job's wish: his own eyes should see his destruction, else it will not touch him, as it did Zedekiah whose children were slain before his eyes.

Keil and Delitzsch note the hapax for 'destruction' (properly a blow) and put the weight on the person-signs: may his own eyes see his ruin, may he himself drink of the divine wrath (the cup of Ps. 75:9). Ellicott reads it as the continuation of Job's suggested amendment of the divine government.

Clarke: he shall perceive its approach and bear the double punishment of fearing and feeling; the cup of God's wrath likened to the poison a criminal must drink (Jer. 25:15, as Socrates); Wesley: to see destruction is to die.
Henry lifts the drinking of the wrath to the world to come, where the eyes wilfully shut against grace are opened to see destruction.

themes: his eyes shall see his destruction
he shall drink of the wrath of the Almighty
justice the sinner himself can feel

schools.summary: Gill: the dead man has no pleasure in his house after him, nor pain in its calamities; he knows nothing of what befalls his family, and asks with the Hebrew what business he has with his house after death.
Henry: the rich man in hell had little pleasure in his house after him, the memory of his good things not cooling his tongue but adding to his misery (Luke 16:25).
Clarke: whatever befalls his posterity he neither knows nor cares, numbered with the dead, his months cut off in the midst; Wesley: what delight in his posterity when he is dying an untimely death?

themes: what pleasure hath he in his house after him
the number of his months cut off
death cuts every cord of interest

schools.summary: Gill: who shall teach the God of knowledge how to govern, telling him whom to afflict and spare? his dealings in providence are not the criterion of men's characters.

Henry resolves the wicked man's varying fate into God's wisdom and sovereignty: he judges those that are high, is accountable to none, and as Judge of all the earth will do right (Gen. 18:25; Rom. 3:6).

Clarke: none can teach God, who teaches the high heavenly ones; the depth is known only to him. Wesley: you teach God when you tell him he must reward and punish in this life; no, he acts as sovereign, with great variety.
Ellicott suggests the words may be the hypothetical reply of Job's antagonist, thrown in and answered, though he leaves the reader free to construe otherwise.

themes: he judgeth those that are high
the sovereignty of the Judge of all the earth

schools.summary: Gill: a man cut off in the very fulness of his vigour, no strength being a security against death; the words may be rendered 'in the strength of his integrity' or perfection.

Keil and Delitzsch render the pair, one dying cheerful and free from care, another in bitterness, the manner of death being no index of character; Ellicott: Job enlarges on the inequality of fate, showing death the only equaliser.
Clarke: the inequality of fortune, health, and strength decides nothing for or against a man; a sudden or a lingering death determines no eternal state.
Henry: wholly at ease and quiet, healthful and vigorous, counting on many years, yet cut off in a moment, as men are taken when they least expect it.

themes: one dieth in his full strength
the manner of death no index of character
cut off at ease and secure

schools.summary: Gill reports the difficulty: some read 'his bowels' or 'sides full of fat,' others (with Broughton) 'his pails are full of milk'; either way a plump, vigorous man not wasted by sickness when death seizes him.
Clarke labours the hapax word, most likely a lost provincial term, and following Parkhurst takes it of the bowels or intestines full of fat (so the Septuagint and Vulgate).
Ellicott judges the uncertain word to mean either milk-pails or the lacteals of the body, the latter suiting the parallelism with the marrow of the bones better.
Henry: healthful and vigorous, of a good constitution like a fat milch cow, counting on many years of mirth and pleasure.

debates.question: How is the hapax word of the first clause to be rendered?

sides.position: milk-pails or vessels of a dairy
the bowels or intestines full of fat, with the Septuagint and Vulgate
the lacteals of the human body, suiting the parallelism

themes: his breasts are full of milk
the marrow of his bones moistened
a body in full health at death

schools.summary: Gill: another wicked man, for there is a difference among them, some happy in life and death, others unhappy in both, dying in bitter pains and black despair, as Judas.
Wesley: another wicked man, so great the variety of God's dispensations, distributing prosperity to one and affliction to another by his wise but secret counsel.
Henry hears an echo of Job's own case: a man dying with much previous pain, in bitterness of soul, never eating with pleasure through sickness, age, or sorrow of mind.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'another dieth in the bitterness of his soul, and hath not enjoyed wealth,' in flat antithesis to the other's abundance.

themes: another dieth in the bitterness of his soul

schools.summary: Gill: they lie down alike in the dust, the worms covering them, no difference between them, until the morning of the resurrection.

Clarke: death levels all distinctions, splendid monuments enshrining corruption but the corpse the same in all; Wesley: worldly differences ended by death, so no man's state can be read from his end, the worm and fire the same to both.
Ellicott: not only the inequality of the wicked man's life is a stumbling-block, but so also is the equality which obliterates all distinction between them in death.
Henry: rich and poor, healthful and unhealthful, meet in the dust, so the differences of this world are not worth perplexing ourselves about.

themes: they lie down alike in the dust
the equality of the grave a second mystery
no verdict from a man's death

schools.summary: Gill grants that the reading of hearts is God's alone, yet a watchful man may guess from look and word; thus Job knew his friends' judgments differed and, for all his proof, they were unconvinced.
Henry: their judgments are tinctured by prejudice and the devices they wrongfully imagine against his comfort and honour, so that such men can hardly be convinced.

Clarke gives the read thought: 'ye still think that because I am afflicted I must be a felonious transgressor'; Wesley: their discourses, though of the wicked in general, are levelled particularly at Job.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'your thoughts and the stratagems with which ye overpower me,' the secret suspicion that Job is an evil-doer reaping the reward of his deeds.
Gill: the very words forming on the friends' lips, appealing to the ruined mansions of great oppressors as proof that God does not let the wicked stand.

Keil and Delitzsch render 'where is the house of the tyrant, and where the pavilions of the wicked?'; Ellicott reads 'prince' as the generous, princely man in antithesis to the wicked, the friends unable to name a crime and so making Job's calamity itself the evidence of a hidden one.
Clarke gives the logic of the taunt: to prove your point you ask, are not the tyrant's houses overthrown, and is that not proof God denies the wicked prosperity?
Henry brings it home: where is Job's own house, and his eldest son's house of feasting? compare it with the dwellings of tyrants, and conclude that Job is such a one.

themes: where is the house of the prince
the dwelling places of the wicked
the friends' argument from Job's fall

schools.summary: Gill: ask any wayfarer met on the road about the true state and character of men, and of Job himself.

Clarke: consult travellers who have gone through different countries, and they will tell you they have seen both examples, prosperity and sudden ruin; Wesley: any passer-by, for it is so common a thing that no man of sense is ignorant of it.
Ellicott glosses 'their tokens' as the marks and evidences of the travellers' experience, the conclusions at which observant men have arrived.
Henry: refer the cause to the next man that comes by; all will agree the punishment of sinners is designed more for the other world (Jude 14; Ps. 92:7).

themes: have ye not asked them that go by the way
punishment reserved for the other world

schools.summary: Gill reads the reserving as a sparing: the wicked are withheld from the calamities that fall on others and kept for eternal destruction, as malefactors reserved for execution, a most dangerous mercy.

Clarke: seeing the wicked prosper, even for a long life, is no proof God loves him, for there he shall meet the day of wrath; Wesley marks the change from singular to plural, that though only some are punished now, then all shall suffer, brought forth as from prison to execution.
Keil and Delitzsch render the travellers' testimony, that the wicked was spared in the day of calamity and in the day of wrath led away.

themes: the wicked reserved to the day of destruction
brought forth to the day of wrath
a stay of execution not an acquittal

schools.summary: Gill notes that some (Jarchi, Aben Ezra) refer the words to God, that none may charge his providence, but himself refers them to the wicked man, so great in wealth as to be above reproof.

Keil and Delitzsch reject the reference to God, since 'who will recompense it to him' is unfitting of God, and with most expositors refer it to the evil-doer, too powerful to be called to account or repaid when he has carried his purpose through.

Clarke: while the wicked is in power none dares tell him his character or repay him, so his punishment must be in another life, for which the day of wrath is prepared; Wesley: his power and splendour are so great that scarce any dares reprove him.
Henry: prosperity sets the sinner above reproof, so that none dares declare his way to his face, and those let alone in sin are marked for destruction (Hos. 4:17).

debates.question: Does 'who shall declare his way to his face?' refer to God, or to the wicked man?

sides.position: to the wicked man, so great that none dares reprove or repay him
to God, whose ways in sparing the wicked none may arraign
holders: Jarchi and Aben Ezra (as reported by Gill)
Ewald and Hirzel (as reported by Keil and Delitzsch)

themes: who shall declare his way to his face
reproof reserved for the day of wrath

schools.summary: Gill: brought to the grave in great funeral pomp, buried honourably in the choicest of his ancestors' sepulchres, and left to remain undisturbed.

Clarke: he dies like other men, the grave preying on him, but reports the Arab notion of a bird issuing from the brain to haunt the tomb; Wesley: the pomp of his death suits his life, an honourable and natural, not a violent, death.

Ellicott presses the word for 'tomb,' elsewhere 'shock of corn' (Job 5:26), so the clause may mean men watch over his sheaves or possessions; Keil and Delitzsch keep the funeral sense, 'over the tomb he still keepeth watch,' the plural amplifying a splendid sepulchre.

debates.question: Does the second clause mean he keeps watch over the tomb, or that men watch over his sheaves (possessions)?

sides.position: he keeps watch over the tomb / grave-mound
men watch over his sheaves, the word meaning 'shock of corn' elsewhere

outliers.note: Reports from Arabic poetry the pagan notion that on a man's death a bird issued from the brain and haunted the sepulchre with a lamentable scream, finding it alluded to in the clause 'he shall watch upon the high-raised heap.'

themes: brought to the grave in state
watch over the tomb or over the sheaves
an honourable burial for the wicked

schools.summary: Gill: the clods of the valley sweet to him, a figure of the utmost repose, feeling no pain and no care for what befalls his posterity.
Keil and Delitzsch render every man drawing after him as innumerable went before; Ellicott: death is robbed of its horror, all glad to join his funeral procession, drawn after him in endless train.

Clarke sees an allusion to a princely burial in a well-watered valley of perpetual spring, emblem of a life to come, and reads 'every man shall draw after him' of death common to all and of the funeral pomp; Wesley: the valley the low, deep grave where he sweetly rests, all after him drawn to die as he did.

themes: the clods of the valley shall be sweet
every man shall draw after him
death robbed of its horror for the wicked

schools.summary: Gill: miserable comforters all, their comfort in vain because it rests on the false maxim that his affliction proves him bad, overthrown by the instances just rehearsed.

Clarke: Job cannot retract, having proved their positions false, and their comfort is as hollow as their doctrine; the chapter is his triumph, a turn from passion to composure. Wesley: why comfort me with vain hopes of recovered prosperity on grounds experience shows to be false?
Ellicott sharpens the last word: what remains in their answers is not merely worthless but 'transgression,' harmful and wrong, a positive fault and not a bare mistake.

themes: how then comfort ye me in vain
in your answers there remaineth falsehood
